summary: Specifies JMAP, a protocol for clients to efficiently query, fetch, and modify JSON-based data objects, with push notification of changes, fast resynchronization, and out-of-band binary upload and download. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) gives clients a consistent way to read and change data on a server. It reduces repeated transfers by batching requests and letting clients fetch only changes.

subtitle: A JSON protocol for reading and changing server data, synchronizing updates, and transferring files.

tldr.problem: Clients need to synchronize data with a server without repeatedly downloading every record or making a separate network request for every action.
tldr.mechanism: JMAP uses authenticated HTTPS requests with JSON method calls. Clients can batch calls, use state strings to fetch changes, transfer binary data separately, and receive push notices that tell them when to synchronize.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8620 defines the generic protocol, while separate specifications define data types. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9404 and RFC 9670.

facts.label: Change history
facts.value: SHOULD cover states given to clients in the last 30 days

facts.label: Unreferenced blob lifetime
facts.value: At least 1 hour, except for quota enforcement

today: RFC 8620 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9404 and RFC 9670; it has not been obsoleted. Its core protocol is generic, and separate specifications define data models.

sections.title: JMAP's Data Model
sections.content:
JMAP is a protocol for synchronizing data such as mail, calendars, and contacts between a client and a server. This RFC defines the shared mechanism; other specifications define the data models that clients synchronize.

Data is organized into accounts. An account can contain several data types, and multiple users may have access to one account. A data type describes named properties, and each individual item of that type is a record with a server-assigned identifier.

Except for binary uploads and downloads, JMAP data uses UTF-8 encoded I-JSON. Every HTTP request must use HTTPS and be authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: JMAP organizes server data into accounts, data types, and records. The core RFC explains how clients exchange those records; separate specifications describe each kind of record.

sections.title: The Session Resource
sections.content:
A client first gets the URL of the JMAP Session resource and credentials. An authenticated GET returns a Session object that lists server capabilities, accessible accounts, and URLs for API requests, file transfer, and push events.

The Session also provides server limits, such as maximum request size and maximum calls in one request. Clients must ignore properties they do not understand and must opt in to capabilities they use. A client may discover the Session through a DNS SRV record and the /.well-known/jmap path.
sections.plainLanguage: The Session response tells a client what the server supports, which accounts it can access, and where to send different requests. The client checks these details before using the service.

sections.title: Batched API Requests
sections.content:
A client sends an authenticated JSON POST to the API URL from the Session. The Request contains a list of method calls, which the server processes in order and answers in the same order.

A later call can refer to a value returned by an earlier call in the same request. This lets the client chain operations without waiting for an extra round trip. Errors can reject the whole request, one method call, or individual record changes; a method-level error does not stop later calls.

Calls in one request run in order, but separate concurrent requests may interleave. Data can therefore change between calls in a single request.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can send several ordered operations in one request. A later operation can use an earlier result, while a failure in one operation does not automatically cancel the rest.

sections.title: Standard Methods and Synchronization
sections.content:
For a data type such as Foo, the common method names are Foo/get, Foo/changes, Foo/set, Foo/copy, Foo/query, and Foo/queryChanges. A type specification says which of these methods that type supports.

get fetches records and a state string. changes returns identifiers created, updated, or destroyed since a known state. set creates, updates, or destroys records; each record change is atomic, although some records can succeed while others fail. Its optional ifInState value can reject a change if the data has moved on.

Servers should be able to calculate changes from states given to clients within the last 30 days. Query methods let clients filter, sort, and select part of a result on the server.
sections.plainLanguage: JMAP uses a small family of methods to fetch records, find changes, edit records, and search. State strings help a client request only the records that changed.

sections.title: Separate Transfer of Binary Data
sections.content:
JMAP keeps binary files outside the JSON API. A blobId identifies immutable raw bytes; a record that uses the blob stores related details such as its name and media type.

A client uploads bytes to the Session's upload URL and receives a blobId. It downloads them from the download URL using the account, blobId, media type, and name. A blob can be reused by other records in the same account, and a server may remove an unreferenced blob after at least one hour, except when quota rules require earlier deletion.
sections.plainLanguage: Binary files use separate upload and download URLs instead of traveling inside JSON requests. A blobId lets a record refer to the file's bytes without sending those bytes again.

sections.title: Push Notices and Resynchronization
sections.content:
A push notification contains a StateChange object with new state strings for changed account data types. The client compares those strings with its own and uses the standard changes methods to fetch details.

JMAP supports a persistent event-source connection and push subscriptions that make the server POST notifications to a client-provided URL. A new subscription must be verified before the server sends further notifications to its URL. Push messages may be combined, and a lost message does not prevent a later synchronization from finding the changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A push notice tells a client which account data may have changed, not the full change itself. The client then requests the missing details from the server.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
JMAP requests must use TLS 1.2 or later, and clients must validate certificate chains. The RFC does not recommend HTTP Basic authentication; if a service uses it, it strongly recommends a separate app password for each client.

Servers must set sensible limits because a small request can cause substantial work or a large response. For push subscriptions, servers must check that URLs are externally resolvable, verify each new URL before sending further notifications, and limit how many subscriptions a user can create. A third-party push service requires encryption keys to protect notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: JMAP protects API traffic with TLS and requires authentication. Servers also limit expensive requests and verify push destinations before sending them notifications.
